title: Поздний банкет для официанток  (A Late Banquet for the Waitresses)

segments.t: At the end of the night, Chef Barinov dismisses the exhausted kitchen crew, only for a waitress to announce that Vika has seated a party of eight VIP guests. After the cooks stay late to prepare the feast, Viktor Petrovich walks into the dining room and finds Vika and the waitresses eating it themselves.
Ещё заказы, пришла компания из восьми человек.
Ну что ж, спасибо вам за поздний ужин.
Let's replay the exchange and look closely at each Russian phrase.
'Alright, single-celled organisms.' Chef Viktor anchors the line on 'like this', while 'single-celled' completes the thought.
'Everyone is dismissed, see you tomorrow.' In Russian, the idea of 'all' flows naturally into 'tomorrow' without extra filler words. Chef Viktor answers right away.
'Bye, everyone.' Here the Russian phrasing highlights 'to everyone' before landing on 'for now'.
Ещё заказы, пришла компания из восьми человек.
'More orders just came in, a party of eight arrived.' Here the Russian phrasing highlights 'else' before landing on 'man'.
'What more orders? It is time to go home.' Here Chef Barinov anchors the thought on 'more, still' and finishes on 'it's time', keeping the spoken rhythm brisk and natural.
'It is time to go home.' Vika brings out the contrast between 'home' and 'it is time' in a few short words.
'But Viktoriya Sergeyevna said.' Chef Viktor anchors the line on 'and', while 'to say' completes the thought.
'That these are very important guests.' Notice how Russian expresses 'what' and 'guests' with crisp inflection rather than helper words. Chef Viktor answers right away.
'Well, just make it quick.' Chef Viktor anchors the line on 'come on', while 'faster' completes the thought.
'Everything tastes so delicious.' In Russian, the idea of 'how' flows naturally into 'deliciously' without extra filler words.
Ну что ж, спасибо вам за поздний ужин.
'Well then, thank you so much for the late dinner.' Notice how Russian expresses 'come on' and 'dinner' with crisp inflection rather than helper words. Vika answers right away.
'Wait, I do not get it.' The '-l' ending on the verb meaning 'understood?' places the action in the masculine past tense.
'Thanks a lot, guys.' Spoken Russian keeps this brisk, leaning on 'kids' and finishing on 'thank you'. Let's hear the complete conversation once more.
Ещё заказы, пришла компания из восьми человек.
Ну что ж, спасибо вам за поздний ужин.

That wraps up this scene as just as the cooks are packing up to go home, Vika orders the kitchen to prepare a late dinner for eight VIP guests—who turn out to be Vika and her waitresses. See you next time!
